issues.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement may be allowed when it assists proper adjudication of the dispute and causes no serious prejudice or loss of an accrued right, even if it adds an alternative defence or is sought after delay.
material_facts: In an eviction suit, the defendant sought to amend its written defence to elaborate its position on the alleged landlord-tenant relationship and to rely on revenue records.

The proposed amendment added an alternative or additional defence; the court found no admission that it sought to withdraw and no accrued right or serious prejudice to the plaintiff that would result.
The plaintiff could respond to the amended written statement, and the proposed amendment was relevant to adjudicating the controversy and avoiding further proceedings.
The application was made after delay, but the court found that delay alone did not establish prejudice.
issues.conclusion: The amendment application should be allowed; the High Court's order setting aside the order allowing the amendment was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, pleadings may be amended when necessary for proper and effective adjudication and to avoid multiplicity of proceedings, subject to the amendment not causing injustice or serious prejudice. A defendant may raise an alternative or additional defence, and the principles governing amendments apply to written statements, with courts generally taking a more generous approach to them. A clear admission conferring a right on the plaintiff is ordinarily not to be withdrawn if doing so would prejudice that right. Delay alone is insufficient to refuse amendment where serious prejudice is not shown and may be compensated. The Court relied on B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameswaran Pillai, A.K. Gupta and Sons Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation, Weldon v. Neal, Charan Das v. Amir Khan, and L.J. Leach and Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_application and (amendment_needed_for_adjudication or amendment_avoids_multiple_proceedings) and no_serious_prejudice and no_accrued_right_is_prejudiced

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A defendant in a civil proceeding applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.amendment_needed_for_adjudication: The proposed amendment supplied material relevant to properly deciding the controversy between the parties.
predicates.amendment_avoids_multiple_proceedings: The proposed amendment could help resolve the dispute without further judicial proceedings.
predicates.no_serious_prejudice: The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious or irretrievable prejudice from the amendment.
predicates.no_accrued_right_is_prejudiced: The proposed amendment was not shown to take away an accrued right of the opposing party.

issues.definition: When a defendant seeks to amend a written statement to assist adjudication or avoid further proceedings, and the amendment causes neither serious prejudice nor loss of an accrued right, the amendment should be allowed.

issues.legal_issue: The High Court's supervisory jurisdiction does not permit it to set aside a subordinate court's order merely to correct an ordinary error when the subordinate court acted within its authority and no grave injustice or fundamental legal failure is shown.
material_facts: A District Judge, exercising revisional jurisdiction, allowed the defendant's application to amend its written statement.
The High Court set aside that order under its supervisory jurisdiction, reasoning that the amendment withdrew an admission and was sought after delay.

The Supreme Court found no admission being withdrawn, no demonstrated prejudice or loss of an accrued right, and no basis to treat the District Judge's order as a jurisdictional failure or a perverse finding.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court had acted as an appellate or revisional court rather than within the limits of supervisory jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction; its order was set aside and the District Judge's order allowing amendment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution imposes a supervisory duty to keep subordinate courts and tribunals within the bounds of their authority, but does not confer an unlimited power to correct ordinary errors or substitute the High Court's judgment for that of a subordinate court. Interference is restricted to serious dereliction of duty, flagrant violation of fundamental principles of law or justice, or findings unsupported by evidence or so perverse that no reasonable person could reach them. The Court relied on Ahmedabad Mfg. & Calico Ptg. Co. Ltd. v. Ramtahel Ramanand, Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, and Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarte.

rule.if: supervisory_challenge_to_subordinate_order and subordinate_court_acted_within_authority and no_serious_dereliction and no_fundamental_violation and no_unsupported_or_perverse_finding

predicates.supervisory_challenge_to_subordinate_ord: A party asked a High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction to set aside an order made by a subordinate court.
predicates.subordinate_court_acted_within_authority: The subordinate court made the challenged order while acting within its legal authority.
predicates.no_serious_dereliction: The subordinate court did not seriously fail to perform its judicial duty.
predicates.no_fundamental_violation: The subordinate court's order did not flagrantly violate a fundamental principle of law or justice.
predicates.no_unsupported_or_perverse_finding: The subordinate court's findings were supported by material and were not so unreasonable that no reasonable court could reach them.

issues.definition: When a subordinate court acts within its authority and has not committed a serious dereliction, fundamental violation, or unsupported or perverse finding, a High Court should not set aside its order through supervisory jurisdiction.
